newsitem.title: USA: U.S. aims to split utilities on nuke waste storage.
newsitem.headline: U.S. aims to split utilities on nuke waste storage.

text.p: The U.S. Energy Department offered to pay individual nuclear utilities for their spent fuel storage costs, if they agreed that the government's delay in removing their radioactive waste was unavoidable, according to a letter released Wednesday.

Under a 1982 law and contracts with utilities, the government was supposed to start taking responsibility for spent fuel from nuclear power plants by the end of January 1998, but the government has nowhere to store it yet.

Utilities banded together and won a lawsuit against the government last year, which forced the Energy Department to declare officially last December that it would be unable to meet its end of the deal.

In a June 3 letter to utilities following up on the court ruling, the Energy Department said it was invoking clauses of the contract that allow for "unavoidable" delays in accepting the spent fuel and allow parties to "mutually agree to amend the contract."
The department gave utilities disputing that the delay was unavoidable 60 days to lay out their arguments on why the delay was avoidable.

For utilities that agreed the delay was not the government's fault and that they were owed no money because of the delay, the department said it was "prepared to address individual contract holders' spent fuel storage concerns."

"Specifically, the Department is willing to consider amendments to individual contracts that would mitigate the impacts of the delay," it said. "Possible amendments could include, for example, compensation for on-site storage costs."
The letter came as a blow to the utilities as a group, which are still fighting the Energy Department in court.

An active lawsuit calls for the government to suspend utilities' annual payments into the federal nuclear waste fund. Electricity consumers have already paid about $10 billion into the fund to build a permanent dump for nuclear waste.
Several utilities told the government earlier this year that the department should not use money from the fund to compensate them for having to keep their spent fuel at their plants beyond 1998.
The Nuclear Energy Institute, which represents nuclear utilities, slammed the Energy Department's latest letter, saying that it was "attempting to duck" its obligations under the law.

"The federal government cannot be allowed to sidestep its responsibility to elctricity consumers who have paid for this program, and then charge taxpayers billions of dollars to pay the penalty for non-performance," said Nuclear Energy Institute President Joe Colvin.

While the Energy Department is trying to settle the dispute with utilities, Congress is debating legislation that would make the government build a temporary storage dump in Nevada for the spent fuel while it continues to investigate a permanent burial site.
